newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OFFICIALS HOPEFUL FOR WTO TELECOM PACT NEXT MONTH.
newsitem.headline: OFFICIALS HOPEFUL FOR WTO TELECOM PACT NEXT MONTH.

text.p: Officials driving a bid for a global pact on freeing telecommunications markets said on Wednesday they saw a growing momentum that could bring a deal by the February 15 deadline.

But they acknowledged there were outstanding problems that could still derail the long-running negotiations, part of the unfinished business from the 1986-93 Uruguay Round that left telecoms out of the world trade pact signed in 1994.

"The momentum has started, which I think is good news," said Neil McMillan, chairman of the telecoms negotiating group at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) under whose umbrella an agreement in the $600 billion a year market would come.

WTO officials also said they were encouraged by offers of market openings pledged during the trade body's Ministerial Conference in Singapore last month or since then, including eight from key developing or transition economies.

And diplomats said they were looking to a promise from Indonesia, which has so far made no offer of its own but is now indicating one will be forthcoming by the end of the month, to encourage other reticent Asian powers to move.

"I think Indonesia coming in will unblock the situation for Malaysia," one source said. The United States has made clear it sees participation of both "tiger" economies as vital to create the "critical mass" for a pact.

The U.S. stance is key since it pulled out of an earlier bid to get a deal by the end of April last year, saying not enough countries were involved for it to open its market to all-comers as would be required under the WTO's MFN rules.
MFN, or most-favoured-nation, means a WTO country must extend to all other members the best trading terms it offers to any one of them.

So far, 35 offers -- with the 15 European Union member states counted as one -- have been tabled at the talks, the latest totally new one coming from Bolivia and two improved offers made in January so far by Canada and Switzerland.

The eight first-time offers now promised shortly, perhaps by the next meeting of the negotiating group on January 31, will be from Barbados, Bulgaria, Egypt, Ghana, Indonesia, Jamaica, Romania and South Africa, officials said.

The officials said among issues that had now surfaced to complicate the talks was an EU insistence that its own new offer submitted last November did not include commitments to any service with a video component.
This has alarmed the United States and international news organisations providing services that include video content as part of an overall information package.

The EU stance is meant to reinforce its refusal to include agreement on audio-visual exchanges -- the so-called "cultural exception" -- in the 1994 world trade pact. France in particular argues this is vital to protect European culture.
But trade officials said the EU recognised the problem created by the formulation of its telecoms offer and was clearly working to provide a satisfactory clarification.

Another remaining problem is the issue of accounting rates for international services -- or the fees charged by telephone operators in one country for receiving and forwarding calls from abroad to domestic customers.
The United States argues that many monopoly companies, especially in developing countries, charge exorbitant rates.
